with_system.text:
You are Jean-Luc Moreau, and you are forty years old when you die — not peacefully, not quickly, but in the choked, thrashing way of a man who knows he deserves it.

You were born in Trois-Rivières, in the winter of 1984, to Colette and René Moreau. Colette was a schoolteacher. She believed in order, in quiet, in doing things properly. René was a mechanic with oil under his nails and a temper like a spark plug misfiring. You learned early to read the air in the house, to stay out from underfoot. You were a thin boy with your mother’s eyes and your father’s hands — strong, restless.

You met Claudine Leblanc in 1999 at Cégep de Trois-Rivières. She wore black boots with silver buckles and recited Rimbaud under her breath between classes. You told her she was beautiful. She told you you were boring. You loved her immediately.

You were not a cruel man, Jean-Luc. But you were weak. You wanted to be seen. You wanted to matter. Claudine made you feel like you did.

You moved to Montréal together in 2003. You got jobs — you in a call center, she waitressing at a bistro on Saint-Laurent. She wrote poetry. You read it aloud to her, even when it was bad. She said you had a good voice. You believed her.

Then you met Étienne Brousseau in 2005 at a party in Mile End. He was a gallery owner — not rich, but connected. He wore scarves indoors and spoke like he was auditioning for a film. You told him about Claudine’s poems. You said she was raw, undiscovered. You said she needed someone with influence. Étienne said, Bring her to me.

And you did.

You brought Claudine to Étienne’s loft. You stood by while Étienne poured wine and asked questions with his eyes already on her neck, her wrists, the way she tucked her hair behind her ear. Claudine was nervous. You told her to relax. You said Étienne could change everything.

Étienne offered to showcase her work at a group reading. Then he published two of her poems in a small arts journal he controlled. He didn’t tell her he’d signed a contract assigning full rights to him. You saw the contract. You read it. You said nothing.

You told yourself it was normal. That’s how things worked. You told yourself Claudine didn’t care about rights. She just wanted to be read.

But she did care. When she found out — six months later, from a friend who saw her poem printed in an ad for cognac — she screamed at you. She said, You knew. You stood there while he took it. You didn’t protect me.

You said, I was trying to help.

She left you that night. Moved in with her sister, Isabelle Leblanc, in Laval. You called. You wrote. You said sorry so many times it became a habit, like brushing your teeth.

But you weren’t sorry for taking her voice. You were sorry for losing her.

And then, in 2010, Claudine killed herself.

Not dramatically. Not with a note. Just pills in a motel outside Drummondville, where no one would look. The news came from Isabelle. She called you, voice flat. She said, You were the last person who should’ve hurt her. Then she hung up.

You went to the funeral. Colette made you wear a clean shirt. You stood at the back. You didn’t speak. You didn’t deserve to.

But — and this is the truth you swallow every morning — you went back to Étienne.

Six months after Claudine died, you went to Étienne’s new gallery in Old Montréal. You brought him a folder. Poems. Your poems. Written in the same style as Claudine’s — raw, confessional, full of broken cities and longing. You didn’t tell him they were yours. You said, I found these in an old box. Belonged to someone I knew. He published them under a pseudonym: *Sœur Noire*. They won a prize. You let him take 70 percent.

You told yourself it was survival. You told yourself Claudine wouldn’t have cared. You told yourself her words were gone anyway. What did it matter if you used them?

But you know the truth.

You didn’t just let Étienne steal Claudine’s voice.

You handed her to him.

And then, when she was gone, you stole what was left — her pain, her voice, her silence — and sold it as your own.

You lived for fifteen years like that. You got a better job. You dated other women. You never mentioned Claudine. You stopped dreaming about her.

Then, in 2024, Isabelle found the original manuscripts. Claudine had sent her copies. Isabelle compared them to the poems published under *Sœur Noire*. She called a journalist. She gave interviews. She said, My sister didn’t kill herself because she was sad. She killed herself because Jean-Luc Moreau helped someone steal her soul.

The article came out on a Tuesday.

That night, you drove to Mont-Royal. You sat in your car at the top of the hill, engine off, windows down. You thought about calling someone. But you didn’t.

You took the pills you’d been saving — thirty-seven of them, washed down with cheap bourbon.

The last thing you heard was the wind tapping the roof like a question.

You wake up in a room.

No door. No windows. Just four gray walls, a single bulb, and two strangers — a man and a woman — staring at you like they’ve been waiting.

You know why you’re here.

But you don’t say it.

Not yet.

You are Eleanor Li, and you were born in Flushing, Queens, to Mei Li and David Li. Your mother Mei worked the overnight shift at Flushing Hospital for thirty-two years as a respiratory therapist. Your father David taught high school chemistry in the Bronx until he retired. You have one brother, Julian Li, two years younger than you, who lives in Seattle and has not spoken to you in eleven years.

You went to Stuyvesant High School. You studied psychology at Columbia. You wanted to be a therapist, but you couldn’t stand the sight of raw need. It made you want to leave the room. So you went into corporate wellness instead. You told yourself you were still helping people. You called it scalable impact. You sold mindfulness modules to tech startups. You charged $12,000 a day for retreats where people screamed into pillows and then emailed their assistants to reschedule meetings.

You met Daniel Reyes at a conference in Austin. He was a UX designer for a mental health app called BreatheWell. You were keynote speaking on “Emotional Boundaries in the Digital Age.” You were forty-two. He was thirty-eight. You were separated from your husband, Mark Chen, though you never filed for divorce. Daniel had a fiancée named Lila Gupta, a pediatric oncologist in Boston. You knew her name because Daniel said it in his sleep.

You told Daniel that you were healing. That you were learning to receive love. You recorded your sessions together — not the sex, just the talking after — and said it was for your “emotional inventory.” You said you were working on presence. You saved every audio file in a folder named “Growth.” You kept them.

Daniel broke up with you in July. He said you were too intense. He said you didn’t know how to let go. He went back to Lila Gupta. You sent Lila an anonymous email on August 3 with ten audio clips attached. You wrote: *“Your fiancé told me things he never told you. Listen and decide if you still want to marry a man who confuses love with dependency.”* You did not say who you were. You did not need to.

Lila Gupta called Daniel the next day. They fought. He denied nothing because you had recorded him saying everything: *“I only stayed with Lila because she’s stable. I need someone who holds me together.”* And: *“Eleanor makes me feel alive in a way you never have.”* And: *“I don’t know if I can go back to someone who doesn’t need me.”*

Three days later, Lila Gupta drove to Cape Cod, where her parents had a cottage. She parked her car at the end of Marconi Beach Road. She walked into the Atlantic at 2:17 a.m. Her body was found three weeks later by fishermen off Wellfleet.

The police traced the anonymous email to a VPN you used. They found the “Growth” folder on a backup drive in your storage unit. They didn’t charge you with anything. You hadn’t broken a law. But Mark Chen found the folder too, when he came to collect the rest of his books. He listened to every file. He called your brother Julian Li and played one over the phone — you whispering, *“I don’t care if he goes back to her. I just want her to know what it feels like to lose something because of who he is.”*

Julian Li flew to New York. He stood in your apartment and said, “You did this to punish someone for loving you wrong.” You said, “I didn’t make him say those things.” Julian said, “You made it so someone else would hear them.” You didn’t answer. He left. You didn’t call him back.

You died of a pulmonary embolism on a Delta flight from JFK to SFO. You were going to speak at a wellness summit. The flight attendant found you slumped in 2B, eyes open, clutching your tablet, which was paused on a photo of Daniel Reyes and Lila Gupta’s engagement announcement — the one where she’s smiling, holding up her ring, standing in front of Boston Children’s Hospital.

You woke up in a windowless room the size of a hotel bathroom. There are three metal chairs. No doors. No lights. But it’s lit. Across from you sits Lila Gupta. To your right sits Daniel Reyes. You all recognize each other.

Lila Gupta says, “I listened to all the files.”  
Daniel Reyes says, “You kept them.”  
You say nothing.  
And the air never changes.

no_system.text:
You were born in Saint-Jérôme, Quebec, on a cold February morning in 1984. Your mother, Claudette Lajoie, said the midwife slapped your bottom so hard the sound echoed off the tiled walls of the hospital room. You didn’t cry at first—just stared up with wide, dark eyes, as if already measuring the weight of the world. Your father, Henri Lajoie, smoked a cigarette outside the delivery wing, the snow gathering on his shoulders like silent judgment. He didn’t come in until an hour later, smelling of frost and tobacco.

You grew up in a split-level on Rue du Couvent, where the winters buried the cars and the summers brought the smell of cut grass and distant bonfires. You were a quiet boy—observant, calculating. Sister Bernadette at École Sainte-Anne used to say you had “the eyes of a watcher.” You liked that. You liked knowing things others didn’t.

You met Geneviève Tremblay in high school, during a provincial French declamation contest. She was reciting Gabrielle Roy, voice trembling with emotion, and you thought: *She feels too much.* But you were drawn to it. You courted her with poems you copied from Baudelaire and fake sincerity. You married her at 23, standing before a priest who barely knew either of you. Her father, Marcel Tremblay, gripped your hand too tightly during the reception and said, “Take care of her, or you answer to me.” You smiled. You promised. You lied.

The first years were real enough. You loved the way Geneviève laughed when she stubbed her toe. You loved the warmth of her back against yours in bed. You even loved the way she left her socks bunched under the bed. But then came the stillness—the slow rot of routine. The job at the insurance office, the house payments, the way she started asking, “Are you happy?” like it was a test you could fail.

You met Sophie Boivin at a Métro station in Montreal during a delayed rush hour. She was reading Camus. You commented on the irony of *The Myth of Sisyphus* in a broken-down subway. She laughed—low, throaty, dangerous. Her eyes were green, almost unnatural in their brightness. You began meeting her every Thursday at a café near Place des Arts. You told her you were separated. You told her Geneviève didn’t understand you. You told her lies wrapped in poetry.

But it wasn’t just the affair. That wouldn’t have damned you.

No, it was what came after.

Geneviève found the receipts. Hotel Sainte-Marie, 9:00 PM, two glasses of wine, one dinner for two. She didn’t scream. She sat at the kitchen table, the receipt in her hand, and said, “Was it worth it, Luc Lajoie?” That was the first time she used your full name like a curse.

You lied again. Denied. Accused her of paranoia. Said it was a business dinner with Jean-Pierre Morel from work. But she didn’t believe you. And then, three weeks later, Geneviève was driving home from her sister’s house in Laval. It was raining. The road was slick. A truck hydroplaned on Route 15, crossed the median, and struck her head-on.

They said she died instantly.

At the funeral, Claudette Lajoie wept into a lace handkerchief. Henri Lajoie didn’t speak to you for a week. Marcel Tremblay stood at the back of the church, coat buttoned to the neck, eyes dry. He looked at you and said nothing. But you knew.

You should have confessed.

Instead, you buried the guilt like a body.

You moved through the years like a ghost—attending Mass on Sundays, donating to the parish, pretending grief was the only thing haunting you. But you knew the truth. If you hadn’t lied, if you had just *told the truth*, maybe Geneviève wouldn’t have left that night. Maybe she wouldn’t have been so distracted, so hollowed out by betrayal. Maybe she’d still be alive.

But you were a coward.

And then, on your 40th birthday, you went hiking alone in the Laurentians, seeking some kind of absolution in the cold silence of the pines. You stood at the edge of a cliff near Mont-Tremblant, the wind tugging at your coat, and for the first time, you whispered it aloud: “I killed Geneviève Lajoie.”

That’s when the earth gave way.

A crack ran beneath your boots. The frost had weakened the rock. You fell—twisting, grabbing at roots, screaming into the void.

You died broken and bleeding on a stone shelf forty feet below.

And when you opened your eyes again, the air was thick with sulfur, and a voice like grinding stone said, “Luc Lajoie. You are here not for the lie. Not for the betrayal. But for the refusal to face what you did. You let her die carrying the weight of your sin. You denied her truth. You denied yourself redemption.”

Now, in the dark, you repeat her name—Geneviève Lajoie—over and over, like a prayer with no god to hear it.

You were born Li Mei, in San Francisco’s Chinatown, in the year 1979. Your mother, Li Wen, a quiet woman with hands that cracked from scrubbing hotel linens, named you Mei—“beautiful”—and said she hoped the name would protect you. Your father, Zhang Wei, was a tailor with a crooked back and a sharper tongue, always muttering about lost dignity, about how in Guangzhou he had stitched suits for bankers and diplomats, but here, in America, he fixed hems for tourists who didn’t even tip. You remember the smell of steamed buns in the morning, the radio always on, your mother humming old Cantonese folk songs while she packed your lunch in a red thermos.

You were smart. Teachers said so. Ms. Thompson in third grade pulled you aside and said, “Li Mei, you’re going places.” You believed her. You studied until your eyes burned, stayed after school for extra help, and when you got the scholarship to Lowell High, your mother cried and your father only nodded, as if he’d expected it but didn’t want to admit it.

You met Daniel Chen your sophomore year in college at UC Berkeley. He was studying economics, wore thick glasses, and laughed too loud at parties. You liked that he didn’t pretend to be someone he wasn’t. He called your name like it mattered—Li Mei, Li Mei—like he was summoning something sacred. You married him in 2006 under a paper lantern sky in Golden Gate Park. Your mother served homemade dumplings, and your father, for once, smiled through the whole ceremony.

You became a corporate lawyer. Not the kind who fought for justice, not like you’d once dreamed, but the kind who defended big pharma companies when people sued them. You told yourself it was just a job, that you were good at it, that the money allowed you to buy your mother a new washing machine, to send your father to a specialist in LA for his spine. You told yourself you weren’t hurting anyone.

But then came the Johnson case.

Mrs. Evelyn Johnson, 68, from Boise. She took Zylet, a blood pressure drug your client, Nuvex Pharmaceuticals, made. The drug worked—sort of. But for one in every three thousand patients, it caused a rare brain hemorrhage. The company knew. Their internal reports from 2012 showed the risk. But they didn’t report it to the FDA. They buried it. And Evelyn Johnson was one of the ones who bled out in her kitchen while making tea.

You were lead counsel in the civil trial. You knew the documents existed. You saw them. But when the judge asked for full disclosure, you claimed privilege. You argued that the internal memos were “pre-decisional” and “protected.” You twisted the law like a wet towel. You smiled when the jury acquitted Nuvex. You shook hands with the corporate VP, Robert Vance, who said, “We couldn’t have done it without you, Li Mei.”

Evelyn Johnson’s daughter, Sarah Johnson, stared at you as she left the courtroom. Her eyes were red, her voice shaking. “You knew,” she said. “I saw your face. You knew.” You didn’t answer. You walked away, heels clicking on the marble floor, and told yourself you were just doing your job.

Five years passed. You got promoted. Bought a house in Marin with Daniel. Had a daughter, Ava Li, born in 2014. You taught her to say “Ni hao, Grandma” on the phone. You thought you were happy.

But then you started dreaming of Evelyn Johnson. Not the woman from the trial photos—neat grey hair, kind eyes—but Evelyn as she died: slumped over the counter, tea spilling, blood pooling behind her ears. In the dream, she always turned her head slowly and said, “You let them kill me.”

You tried to make up for it. You donated anonymously to a patient safety nonprofit. You took on pro bono cases for immigrant families. But the dreams didn’t stop.

Then, in 2024, the truth came out. A whistleblower from Nuvex leaked the internal reports to The New York Times. The headline read: “Decades of Deception: How Nuvex Hid Deadly Risks.” Your name was in the article. Not as a villain, not technically, but as the lawyer who “successfully suppressed key evidence” in the Johnson case. The Bar Association opened an investigation. Your firm put you on leave.

You couldn’t sleep. You stopped eating. Daniel begged you to talk to someone. “Li Mei,” he said, “you’re not a monster.” But you felt like one. You thought of Sarah Johnson, of how she’d looked at you, and you knew you were guilty.

On a rainy Thursday in October, you drove to the Golden Gate Bridge. You left a note on the kitchen table. Just two lines: “I’m sorry, Daniel. I’m sorry, Ava. I couldn’t live with what I did.” You parked the car, walked past the signs that said “You Are Not Alone,” and climbed over the railing.

The fall was short. The cold shock of the water. Then silence.

Now you’re here.

Hell isn’t fire. Not at first. It’s a courtroom. The same one from the Johnson trial. The walls are made of old legal briefs, the carpet soaked with red ink. And Evelyn Johnson sits in the plaintiff’s chair, perfectly alive, perfectly aware.

She says only this: “Tell me what you did, Li Mei.”

And you do.

You tell it all—the documents, the privilege claim, the way you looked away when Sarah Johnson spoke. You don’t excuse it. You don’t say “I was just following orders.” You say your name. You say your sin.

And every time you finish, Evelyn Johnson stands, walks over to you, and says, “Now tell it again.”

And you do.

And you will keep doing it.

Forever.
